transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-16
Start time: 14:30 PDT
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Oscar (RWD SE), Liam (Asteria SRE), Priya (Asteria Platform), Nora (Asteria Product), Samir (Asteria Security)

Summary: quick deep-dive into Redwood’s diagnostics and "pathfinder" approach to mapping inference errors back to origin requests, KV-cache behavior, and fallthrough routing. Customer wanted concrete next steps to run a short pilot and validate latency/cost tradeoffs with their retail query workload.

Topics: product tracing, request-level logs, error classification, KV cache hits, fallback to cheaper models, VPC/on-prem constraints, SOC2/KMS, pilot plan and timelines.

-- Transcript --
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick audio check — can you hear me?
[00:05] Liam (Asteria): Yep, loud and clear.
[00:07] Priya: Good here.
[00:09] Jordan: Cool. I'm Jordan, AE on the account, with Maya and Oscar from the SE team. Today we want to walk through how Redwood surfaces inference diagnostics — basically map a user-visible error back to the exact token turn, model variant and infra path. We'll show some live examples and then discuss pilot steps.
[00:27] Maya (Redwood SE): Hi folks. I'll start with a quick overview of the tracing surface — think of three signals: request meta (headers, route, model config), execution trace (batch placement, kernel path, kv cache hits) and application-level outcome (response tokens, error codes, latency). We stitch those in the console into a single timeline.
[00:45] Priya: When you say KV cache hits, do you mean like prefix caching? We use a lot of session-based prompts, so 80% of requests hit a common prefix.
[00:53] Maya: Yes, prefix and KV — though internally we sometimes say "KV cash" in older logs, haha, the transcription shows that. But yes, you should see a hit ratio metric per request and per model.
[01:03] Nora: Are those metrics real-time? We need to debug production flares.
[01:07] Oscar: They are near-real-time — typically 2–3s aggregation in the console UI, with request-level markers streaming for each request if you enable the verbose trace flag.
[01:17] Samir (Asteria Security): Quick security question — if we enable verbose traces, do those include PII from requests? We need to ensure logs are redacted and KMS keys stay in our control.
[01:26] Maya: Good callout. By default we mask tokens and apply heuristics; for production private deployments we integrate with customer KMS and you can opt into redaction rules. We also support retention controls per route.
[01:36] Liam: Ok, demo please?
[01:38] Jordan: Yep, Maya will share screen.
[01:42] [01:42] Maya: (shares) Alright, this is a synthetic retail session we onboarded — example query: "Find cheapest alternative to product X with delivery before Friday". You can see the request tile, the model used, and the route config.
[01:58] [02:00] Maya: In the timeline here's the request start, we show batching window, assigned worker, and a small orange flag — that indicates a tokenization mismatch that caused a retry.
[02:10] Priya: Sorry what caused the retry? Was that from our client or the runtime?
[02:14] Maya: Good question. This was the runtime tokenizer mismatch — we had a model variant with slightly different tokenizer vocabulary after a quantization conversion. In the console it's annotated as "tokenization fallback" with the worker id.
[02:24] Liam: That seems bad — how often does that happen? We saw a 0.3% error spike last week and weren't sure where it came from.
[02:31] Oscar: Tokenization mismatches are uncommon; they're most often during model swap rollouts or when a model has a post-quantize export change. Part of the rollout toolchain is a preflight tokenizer check — we'll show how to surface those failures and auto-rollback.
[02:45] [02:45] Maya: I'm clicking into the request detail — here's the raw request, masked outputs, and an execution trace with KV cache hit: 0.42 on the prefix. You can also see the kernel path selection — we chose the fused attention kernel because sequence length was small.
[03:00] Priya: I'm seeing an odd thing in the trace where batch size is 1 but there's a batching window of 50ms — what's the tradeoff?
[03:07] Maya: So Redwood uses continuous batching; the window is to allow throughput gains when spikey traffic arrives. You can tune per-route SLOs — if you want 99th percentile latency < 120ms you can tighten batching windows or pin a lower-latency pool.
[03:20] Nora: What does that do to cost?
[03:22] Oscar: Lower batching windows increases cost because you lose some efficiency. We can model that with your sample traces — we'll include that in the pricing sheet.
[03:33] [03:33] Priya: About fallbacks — you said we can route to cheaper variant on overload. If a request falls back mid-token, how do you guarantee output consistency?
[03:42] Maya: We don't switch model mid-generation. Fallbacks happen at request start — either we route to a compatible variant or queue for a higher tier. For long-running streams we support graceful degrade: continue with a cached prefix or a distilled variant if compatible embeddings are maintained.
[03:56] Liam: Our main concern is semantic drift — cheaper variant returning different answers is a risk for us.
[04:01] Jordan: Totally, that's why we recommend a canary rollout and run A/B quality evals on your golden prompt set. Redwood Optimize gives automated regression alerts if quality drops below threshold.
[04:12] [04:12] Nora: Can we see the console view for a request that actually failed with a 500 and an explained root cause?
[04:18] Maya: Sure — opening an older incident. The UI shows a stack: request -> worker -> kernel -> runtime exception. You can click the exception and see the heap dump snippet (sanitized) and the runtime logs tied to the same timestamp. There's also a suggested remediation: increase model heap or switch to a multi-worker config.
[04:37] Samir: Are runtime logs stored in our VPC or in Redwood's storage? We need to know for compliance.
[04:42] Maya: For private deployments logs can stay in your VPC and we ship only metadata to the control plane. For hosted API we retain logs encrypted at rest and they are pseudonymized; SOC2 report covers our controls.
[04:55] Priya: How do you correlate app-level errors back to upstream infra? We have a service mesh and want to map a user session id across systems.
[05:03] Oscar: We ingest your x-request-id headers and stitch them; the console supports custom correlation keys and will surface them in traces. There's also a downloadable JSON export for each trace.
[05:14] Liam: That JSON export — does it include the model weights or anything sensitive?
[05:18] Maya: No model weights ever. The export contains the request meta, timing, and anonymized logits if you opt in for debugging. We can redact tokens by policy.
[05:28] [05:30] Priya: Can we run a 2-week pilot where we route a subset of traffic through Redwood Dedicated and compare latency/cost?
[05:36] Jordan: Yes. Our usual approach: spin up a small Dedicated pool in our staging region, replicate your routing rules, and replay 24–72h of sample traffic at scale. We'll run benchmarks with and without cache priming to show delta.
[05:48] Priya: About VPC peering — we use strict egress rules. How does the Dedicated talk to our VPC?
[05:54] Maya: We support VPC peering and private endpoints; traffic can remain on your network for private deployments. For Dedicated we can offer either customer-managed VPC peering or a managed VPN tunnel depending on network constraints.
[06:06] Samir: KMS integration — do you support HSM-backed keys?
[06:09] Oscar: Yes, HSM/KMS integrations are supported for Private. For hosted we maintain keys but can offer customer-managed keys in certain enterprise tiers.
[06:19] [06:20] Jordan: Quick detour — competitors. We've heard you evaluating Anthropic and a homegrown solution?
[06:27] Liam: Anthropic for safety controls, and we have an internal endpoint for low-risk tasks. Anthropic's latency is a bit higher for our region.
[06:33] Jordan: Ok, good to know. We'll highlight our latency vs cost profile and how tracing differentiates us — especially request-correlation and KV metrics that help you prevent recurring failure modes.
[06:43] [06:45] Maya: I'm going to simulate a fallthrough event: request comes in, primary variant overloaded, we trigger fallback to a distilled variant. Here you can see a diff view comparing tokens returned between the two variants and an automated quality delta score.
[06:58] Nora: That delta score — is it BLEU or something custom?
[07:01] Maya: It's a composite: semantic similarity (embedding cosine), token overlap and a heuristic for hallucination risk trained on Redwood evals. We'll share the metric docs after the call.
[07:11] Priya: One more thing — retention. We only want to keep request traces for 30 days to satisfy our data policy.
[07:17] Oscar: That's configurable per-route. For private installs you can enforce retention via our config and lifecycle hooks.
[07:24] [07:25] Liam: Can you run the benchmark with our flash-sale pattern? We have lots of short queries at 100ms inter-arrival and big bursts.
[07:33] Maya: Yes, please upload the trace dump; we'll run both warm and cold cache scenarios. The warm cache shows large savings due to prefix KV hits.
[07:43] Priya: On the upload: do you have a secure drop? We prefer S3 with pre-signed URLs.
[07:47] Jordan: We'll send a pre-signed S3 link via the deal folder.
[07:50] [07:50] Samir: Last compliance question — any certifications beyond SOC2? ISO? Pen test reports?
[07:56] Jordan: We have SOC2 and we publish pen test summaries; ISO as an addendum on roadmap for certain regions. We'll attach the latest security pack.
[08:05] Oscar: I'm going to show an example export now — here's the trace JSON: top-level keys include request_id, correlation_keys, timeline events, worker_id, kernel_path, cache_hits, and error annotations. This is the file we'd use for deeper offline analysis.
[08:21] Priya: Nice.
[08:23] [08:23] Maya: A quick note on observability: the Console also surfaces per-token latency waterfall which is super helpful for spotting slow decoding kernels; you can then pin to a different GPU kernel or enable fused kernels depending on model.
[08:36] Liam: Great. So next steps recap?
[08:39] Jordan: From Redwood side: 1) we'll provision a small Dedicated staging cluster and share creds by 2026-07-20; 2) Maya will run KV-cache + batchability benchmarks with your trace and send results by 2026-07-23; 3) Oscar will attach the security pack and SOC2 summary. From Asteria: upload trace dump and SAML metadata by 2026-07-19.
[09:02] Priya: That timeline works.
[09:04] Nora: One ask — can you include a sample rollback playbook for tokenization/rollout failures? We want a clear runbook.
[09:11] Maya: Absolutely, we'll include a canary rollback playbook and a checklist for tokenizer preflight.
[09:16] [09:17] Jordan: Anything else before we close?
[09:18] Liam: No — thanks, that was helpful and concrete.
[09:21] Priya: Thanks, appreciate the operational detail.
[09:23] Samir: Thanks — we'll review security pack and follow up with any gaps.
[09:26] Jordan: Great, we'll follow up with the S3 link and the pricing/benchmark artifacts.
[09:30] Meeting end.

Questions captured: 
- How does Redwood redact PII in verbose traces?
- What metrics constitute the quality delta for fallback variants?
- How do we configure retention per-route?
